mission.h2: Build tools that listen to the recording itself.
mission.body1: The ability to tell a story through sound is a deeply human trait. Woven into the history of our species, music connects people and intensifies emotion in ways few other art forms can.
mission.body2: With Resomix, we are building a platform that works beyond tags, popularity signals and static metadata. It starts from the audio recording and uses measurable sonic characteristics to support discovery and understanding.
mission.body3: By analysing structure, harmony, rhythm, timbre, spectral character and energy, Resomix opens three distinct routes: find sonically related tracks, examine one recording in greater detail, or make an authorised catalogue searchable by sound.
mission.interp: Metadata tells us what a recording is called. Audio analysis gives us another way to understand how it moves, feels and relates to other recordings.
mission.figureAria: A metadata frame — title, artist, genre, release date, label — surrounds the audio-derived evidence: five characteristic bands and seventy-plus measurable characteristics.

evidence.h2: Music discovery should go deeper than tags and trends.
evidence.body1: Resomix began with a frustration familiar to DJs, curators and music professionals: spending hours moving through stores, platforms and catalogues to find the recording that fits a particular moment.
evidence.body2: PYXIS-1, our proprietary audio-analysis and similarity engine, preprocesses recordings and extracts more than 70 measurable characteristics across rhythm, harmony, timbre, structure, spectral profile and energy.
evidence.body3: It creates a sonic profile that can be read through Track Intelligence or compared with recordings already processed into an applicable index. Similarity results are ranked automatically according to the closest measured sonic relationships.
evidence.status: Proprietary algorithm · Audio-derived evidence · Human decision
evidence.figureAriaD: One recording enters; five characteristic bands and seventy-plus characteristics form one sonic profile; the profile supports two possible operations — read one recording through Track Intelligence, or compare with an index for ranked similarity.
evidence.figureAriaM: Mobile: one recording, five bands, one sonic profile, two possible operations.

evolution.h2: One human problem. Three distinct ways to work with sound.
evolution.intro: The first question was simple: if one track feels right, what should come next? Building that discovery engine revealed two further needs — understanding the recording in greater detail and bringing the same sound-first search into authorised catalogues.

vision.h2: Make sound itself a route into discovery.
vision.body1: We want to make analysing and discovering music faster and more useful. We imagine a world where a recording’s visibility is not determined only by chart position, marketing budget, recency or the accuracy of its tags.
vision.body2: Resomix builds a sonic profile from measurable characteristics and uses it to reveal relationships that metadata alone may not show. The aim is not to replace listening, taste or professional judgement. It is to help them travel further.
vision.statement: The recording deserves another way to be found.

principles.h2: Measurable sound. Clear outputs. Human judgement.
principles.intro: Resomix combines proprietary processing and ranking with established audio-analysis tools to create a practical sonic profile for each recording.

p1.title: Audio-derived evidence
p1.body: PYXIS-1 works from the recording, extracting more than 70 measurable characteristics across verified sonic dimensions.

p2.title: Read or compare
p2.body: A sonic profile can support a readable Track Intelligence view or be compared with an applicable pre-analysed index. These are distinct workflows.

p3.title: Results in seconds
p3.body: Existing indexed references return faster. Uploaded references take longer because they must first be processed. Similarity results are ranked automatically.

p4.title: Human decision
p4.body: Resomix surfaces evidence and candidates. DJs, producers, curators and catalogue teams make the final call.

chainNote.body: Every returned result can become a new starting point after the playlist has been delivered, allowing a listener to follow a new sonic direction without changing how the original ranking was created.

shelf.h2: Relevance should not expire with release date.
shelf.body1: Every catalogue has a quieter layer — tracks that did not reach the charts, albums that fell through algorithmic cracks and artists whose work sits outside the spotlight.
shelf.body2: Resomix can bring a recording back into view when it is sonically relevant to a reference. It does not predict commercial success or guarantee exposure. It creates another evidence-based route into discovery.
shelf.figureAriaD: Rows of catalogue recordings arranged by release order; one older recording receives a sonic relationship from the active reference and moves into the ranked output row, its release date visible.

values.h2: Technology should expand human listening — not pretend to replace it.

v1.title: The art of personal curation
v1.body: You still make the call. Resomix helps you get there faster by surfacing candidates and evidence that support deeper listening.

v2.title: Another route for less-visible music
v2.body: Sound-first retrieval can give older and lower-exposure recordings another chance to surface when they are relevant to a reference.

v3.title: Clear boundaries
v3.body: Temporary user references and partner catalogue assets follow separate handling paths. Each partner catalogue and sonic index remains inside its authorised scope.

v4.title: Precision over volume
v4.body: Resomix returns ranked results and lets the user choose the available result depth. More results are not automatically better results.

team.body1: Resomix was born from a frustration familiar to many music professionals: spending hours exploring platforms and catalogues to find the music needed for a project or DJ set.

founder.quote2: Resomix is the tool I needed and could not find: built on signal processing, not hype. After creating our discovery engine, I realised people across the music sector could benefit from the same foundation — not only DJs, but also producers, supervisors, publishers and catalogue owners. Resomix is designed to show connections and enhance human curation across the industry.”

product.h2: One processed catalogue. Two verified outputs.
product.body: Catalogue Intelligence is the catalogue-scale application of PYXIS-1. Once authorised recordings have been processed, each track can participate in discovery in two ways: as a reference that starts a search and as a candidate that can be returned when its sonic relationship is strong.
product.outABody: Submit an indexed track or an approved audio reference and receive the closest matches from the partner catalogue, ordered by PYXIS-1 similarity.
product.outBBody: Retrieve the analysis of a processed recording across rhythm, harmony, timbre, structure, spectral character and energy when a closer examination is required.

flow.h2: Start with one track. Return relevant recordings from your own index.
flow.body1: A catalogue track can use its stored sonic profile immediately. An authorised uploaded reference is processed first. PYXIS-1 then compares that reference with the prepared partner index and returns the closest catalogue matches in ranked order.
flow.body2: The system does not ask the user to build the result list manually, and it does not reanalyse every candidate during each search.
flow.figureAriaD: Two input routes — an indexed catalogue track using its existing profile, or an authorised reference upload profiled before comparison — converge into one reference profile, are compared with the partner index, and return automatically ranked results.
flow.figureAriaM: Mobile flow: the two input routes converge into one reference profile, compared with the partner index, returning automatically ranked results.

trackIntel.h2: Open Track Intelligence when you need to understand the recording in greater detail.
trackIntel.body1: Similarity answers “what is sonically related?” Track Intelligence answers “what does PYXIS-1 detect in this recording?” For a processed track made available within the partner scope, the analysis can present structural, harmonic, rhythmic, timbral, spectral and energy characteristics.
trackIntel.body2: This is a separate analysis view. It is not repeated beside every similarity result, and the user does not need to inspect it before receiving ranked matches.
trackIntel.figureAriaD: A wide Track Intelligence inspection panel for one fictional recording: structural waveform with labelled sections, energy journey, tempo and harmonic fields, and a restrained timbre view.
trackIntel.figureAriaM: Mobile Track Intelligence preview with structure, energy, tempo, harmonic and timbre fields.

value.h2: Let sonic relevance give deeper catalogue another route into discovery.
value.body1: Metadata, release schedules and editorial priorities remain essential. PYXIS-1 adds a different retrieval signal: the relationship inside the audio itself. When an older, niche, new or unreleased recording is close to the reference, it can be returned because of that relationship—not because it already has behavioural history or recent attention.
value.body2: Resomix does not predict demand, guarantee exposure or decide what should be promoted. It makes more of the authorised catalogue eligible to be found when it is relevant to the sound being searched.
value.mod1Body: Relevant older recordings can appear beside newer releases when PYXIS-1 ranks the sonic relationship strongly.
value.mod2Body: New or unreleased audio can be profiled and matched without waiting for streams, sales or interaction history.
value.mod3Body: One known recording can lead users or internal teams into relevant catalogue inventory they might not have reached through metadata alone.

value.figureAriaM: Mobile: the recent active reference and the older catalogue recording connected by one sonic relationship; the older recording appears in the ranked results.

partner.h2: Add sonic retrieval without replacing the systems you already run.
partner.body1: Resomix is designed as a complementary discovery and analysis layer. During a guided pilot, partners can test catalogue similarity and Track Intelligence on an agreed sample. In a scoped integration, authorised server-side requests can retrieve similarity or analysis responses for use inside the partner’s own product or internal workflow.
partner.body2: The partner retains its catalogue, brand, licensing model and customer relationship. Resomix supplies the processing, sonic profiles, ranking and response layer defined in the agreement.
partner.figureAriaD: Four-part architecture: the partner product or internal tool calls scoped API access, which reaches the partner sonic index and returns either ranked similarity results or a track analysis response.
partner.figureAriaM: Mobile integration: partner product, scoped API access, partner sonic index, then the two response branches.

boundary.h2: Your private catalogue does not become a shared partner pool.
boundary.body1: Authorised catalogue audio, derived profiles and the searchable index are restricted to the applicable partner scope. One partner’s private content is not exposed as another partner’s catalogue result. Access, retention and deletion follow the relevant written agreement.
boundary.body2: Partner catalogue processing begins only with authorised audio and metadata supplied for the agreed service.

boundary.figureAriaM: Mobile: the two partner indexes stacked and fully separate, each with its own key, query and results.

hero.intro: Running a label is hard, and it always has been. Choosing the artists to release, curating every project with care, managing a growing catalogue, and consistently releasing music that's in line with the essence of your project all require time and dedication.
hero.figureAria: Ten years of a label's releases drawn as a timeline; one orange thread connects a recent signing back to an older release, re-lighting it

statement.body: A carefully crafted similarity engine not only helps diversify a label's output, but also identifies new opportunities for the label and its roster. When chosen right, this is a tool that becomes an invaluable companion — one that can expand the visibility of any creative project.

metadata.p1: As a record label grows, it needs tools to help it search, organise, and understand its catalogue. It might be easier to do it all manually with a catalogue of 10, 20, or 50 releases. But what about 100, or 200?
metadata.p2: With these numbers, it's easy to lose sight of a project's narrative, or miss opportunities that'd increase the label's visibility. A forgotten track published years ago that'd be a perfect fit for a movie soundtrack, or an older release could find a new audience through its sonic similarity to a recent signing.
metadata.p3: Metadata helps, but it doesn't describe how music actually sounds, which makes connections difficult to find.
metadata.figureAria: The same catalogue seen two ways: as a flat metadata table where every row looks alike, and as a sonic field where tracks group by how they sound and a forgotten release stands out

quote.text: "A similarity engine that truly understands our catalogue could help us explore new directions, diversify our output organically, and introduce older releases to new audiences while highlighting the depth of our work over the past decade."
quote.name: Marco Alessi

workflows.h2: Built for the label's working week
workflows.lead1: Resomix analyses the audio itself, allowing labels to search and compare music based on sonic similarity instead of simply using metadata.
workflows.lead2: In the day-to-day management of a label, this process makes it easier to:

items.demo: Understand how new demos fit within an existing catalogue.
items.dormant: Rediscover forgotten releases and put them in front of a new audience.
items.cluster: Build compilations or playlists around a cohesive sound, in no time.

workflows.close: Instead of relying on memory and manual listening, you can now explore new possibilities within your catalogue, built through years of dedication and hard work.

creativity.h2: Sonic analysis at the service of creativity
creativity.p1: By making entire catalogues searchable purely by sound, a label team spends less time searching and more time discovering. In this case, the difference between these two similar terms is vital.
creativity.p2: Our deterministic engine can do the heavy lifting, highlighting opportunities for your label that might have been ignored. Your role, whether you're the label founder or marketing assistant, will always be to choose the right path for the label based on its history and creative integrity.
creativity.p3: Resomix's similarity engine is not designed to replace the human "touch", but to enhance it and amplify it so that it can reach its true potential.

editorial.p1: That’s no trivial task, especially if you consider that your average catalog hosts tens of thousands of songs!
editorial.p2: The good thing is that technology comes to the rescue with automating systems that help search, analyze, and optimize large catalogs in ways no human can; only these powerful engines can dive into a music collection so deeply and thoroughly, delivering results in line with what you’re looking for.
editorial.pull: But there’s something only the finest discovery engines can do: translate emotions and moods into sonic connections.
editorial.afterQuote: Resomix was designed to do precisely that.

gap.h2: A Big Catalog Is Not Enough – When You Don’t Know It
gap.p1: Spending years building a catalog, only to barely touch its true potential, is the problem of every music publisher today.
gap.p2: The story usually goes like this: new releases are prioritized, while older songs slowly disappear from view. That’s partly intrinsic to the modern music industry, where new songs are more sought-after, whereas songs that are not old enough to be considered vintage live in this limbo where no one looks for them.
gap.p3: Metadata can help rediscover songs buried in a catalog, but it’s not designed to see sonic connection: it shows you songs that are tagged the same way, but that doesn’t mean they’re sonically related, or that they can fill the same purpose. What you need is an engine specifically designed to explore your entire catalogue through the sound itself.
gap.figureAriaD: A catalogue timeline with three zones — established workhorses, a large quiet underexposed middle, and recent visible releases. A metadata rail sits above; a sonic relationship layer sits below. One orange path bypasses the metadata grouping and connects a recent reference to a work inside the underexposed middle.
gap.figureAriaM: Mobile: the three catalogue zones stacked, with the metadata rail above, the sonic layer below, and one orange path connecting a recent reference to an underexposed work.

activate.p1: Resomix analyzes the structure of a song at a granular level, going deeper than any search engine and extrapolating the core of a song, its sonic soul.
activate.p2: This allows publishers to explore and compare compositions based on their sonic characteristics rather than simply relying on metadata. By analysing the structural, harmonic, rhythmic, timbral, and emotional qualities of a track, Resomix’s proprietary engine PYXIS-1 can uncover relationships between compositions that are not audible at first glance, but are undoubtedly there.

statement.body: Having thousands of samples, loops, presets, and sounds gives producers an almost infinite number of creative possibilities. The perfect sound might already be there, simply buried underneath hundreds of similar results.
statement.engine: A carefully crafted similarity engine not only helps users find sounds faster, but also gives them new ways to explore a catalogue they might otherwise never fully discover.

tags.p1: Most sample libraries rely on metadata to help users navigate their catalogues. Genre, instrument, BPM, key, mood and other tags are helpful, but they can only describe a sound up to a certain point.
tags.p2: Two drum patterns might both be tagged as "electronic", but sound completely different. Two vocal samples might both be described as "emotional", while having very little in common sonically.
tags.p3: The problem is even more apparent when a producer doesn't know exactly what they're looking for: maybe a synth texture like one they heard in another track, or a drum loop that has the same energy as their reference, but they don't know what to search for.

hero.intro: Learning to DJ might not sound that difficult. Becoming a great DJ, however, is an entirely different matter.
hero.figureAria: A crate of records drawn as dense rows of spines; one record is pulled out and a journey of ranked musical ideas unfolds from it — ideas, not a set order

statement.p1: The best DJs are not only creative in their selection, but also consistent in terms of style and performance quality. At the end of the day, the not-so-secret formula to DJing mastery is to craft your own sonic identity, and never stop evolving and refining your sets.
statement.p2: This is easier said than done, though. Once they start playing regularly, it becomes increasingly harder for DJs to present different sets every night, which leads them to use the same tracks over and over. This, in turn, makes their sets predictable, less engaging, and "cold". Plus, every hour spent digging through folders, playlists and tags is time that could be spent discovering new musical directions instead.
statement.engine: A refined similarity engine, specifically designed to analyse a music catalogue to deliver accurate and unexpected results, might be the best way to avoid repetitiveness and speed up the curation process.

library.h2: A DJ's biggest asset is also their biggest problem
library.p1: I'm of course talking about the DJ's music library.
library.p2: It's not uncommon for a professional DJ to have tens of thousands of songs saved on the hard drive. It's impossible for the human mind to remember them all, let alone see the connections between them!
library.p3: The result is that a vast majority of a DJ's collection gets lost, buried underneath the latest entries to their library and the unmissable signature songs they always play on stage.
library.p4: Within those thousands of forgotten songs are hidden gems: tracks you heard once and bought on a whim years ago, or unknown b-sides only a handful of people know exist.
library.pull: What if, among that ocean of forgotten tracks, there's a perfect fit for the mood of your next DJ set?
library.p5: When relying exclusively on tagging and cataloguing systems, results can be hard to analyse because tags, even when perfectly fine-tuned, are not enough to describe a song's emotional impact.
library.p6: What you need is a sonic analysis layer designed to understand the complexity of modern music libraries; one that, instead of searching by genre, artist, label or manually assigned tags, makes the music itself the search query.
library.figureAria: A DJ library drawn as depth: the latest entries bright at the top, the signature songs pinned, and a vast dim middle where three hidden gems faintly glow

journeys.h2: Turning music folders into sonic journeys
journeys.lead1: Enter Resomix, a sonic similarity engine that reads the sonic DNA of a reference track by analysing its rhythmic, harmonic, timbral, structural and emotional characteristics. Instead of following metadata blindly, Resomix's deterministic engine PYXIS-1 uses the music itself to open new sonic paths across your library.
journeys.lead2: For a DJ, this means making the most not only of your unique taste and style, but also of the vast catalogue that took you years to build.
journeys.lead3: Furthermore, what used to take hours of manual digging can now happen in seconds. Pick a single track that captures the mood you're looking for, and Resomix instantly returns a ranked collection of tracks that are sonically related to it. Instead of starting every search from scratch, you'll have a curated set of creative possibilities at your disposal, right away.
journeys.intro: Some examples of the improvements Resomix can bring to your workflow:

rediscover.label: Rediscover forgotten tracks
rediscover.text: Bring those hidden gems back into your sets. A forgotten B-side released years ago and a recent release might perfectly fit each other, if their sonic relationship is strong.

connections.label: Find unexpected connections
connections.text: Go beyond your existing tagging system and discover relationships that genres and manually assigned tags cannot reveal.

escape.label: Escape repetition
escape.text: Explore new musical directions and stop relying on the same dozen tracks.

prepare.label: Prepare sets faster
prepare.text: Spend less time searching through folders and more time focusing on the "journey" of your set.

journeys.pull: Resomix doesn't build a set from scratch, but it does remove the slow search process, giving you dozens of musical ideas in seconds while leaving the creative decisions to you.

unique.p1: There's something about a DJ's style that automation simply can't replicate. Your ability to read the room and mix tracks seamlessly is the core of your musical identity, and Resomix's similarity engine is here to make your discovery process faster, more creative, and intuitive.
unique.p2: Our deterministic engine is a creative companion, one that won't replace your unique taste, but rather help you discover more possibilities, faster, so you can spend less time searching and more time shaping the music journey you want to create.
unique.figureAria: The room drawn as a soft arc of listeners above; the DJ, a white ring, stands between the room and a fan of surfaced musical ideas — the engine suggests, the DJ reads the room

hero.intro: The art of music curation is born from a unique mix of talent and experience; the ability to hear music differently, to predict trends, to see hidden connections, is the essence of what makes humans connect through music.
hero.figureAria: Tracks scattered across decades and genre strata; from the reference track a signal journey flows outward through numbered stops across eras and genres — a playlist chain linked by the curator, with one direction still unexplored

statement.p1: To stay on top of the game as a music curator requires a clear process and the right tools that can help you uncover hidden gems among the thousands of songs released daily. Especially when you have a clear sonic identity in mind, having the ideal discovery engine at your disposal can help bring your creative vision to life.
statement.engine: With Resomix, a reference track becomes a starting point to explore multiple directions that would be difficult to find through traditional discovery methods — quickly, creatively, and based on the emotions that music conveys.

gap.h2: Recommendations will only take you this far
gap.p1: We all rely on recommendations, whether they come from our pals or the algorithm of our favourite streaming platform. They're invaluable, and can help you discover new things every day.
gap.p2: The problem with human recommendations is that we're limited by the time it takes to actually listen to and appreciate music. On the other hand, the issue with algorithms is that they're not good at lateral thinking, making them less effective when you want to break barriers between genres and explore new sounds.
gap.p3: These two approaches to music discovery are critical, but neither can provide the depth of discovery that a curator sometimes needs. What's missing is a workflow that combines the best of both: the "soul" of human sonic discovery, and the powerful research engines that modern algorithms can provide.
gap.figureAria: Two beams of discovery: human recommendations reach deep but narrow, platform recommendations reach broad but shallow; between them lies missed territory with faint gems, and an orange beam reaches into it

rail.lead1: What curators need is a discovery engine that analyses the audio itself, without relying on metadata, giving them a fresh approach to the music they find and select for their projects.
rail.lead2: By analysing the structural, harmonic, rhythmic, timbral, and emotional qualities of a reference track, PYXIS-1 is designed to discover new connections between songs, hidden underneath the surface of the genres the songs naturally fall into.

philosophy.h2: Sonic analysis at the service of creativity
philosophy.p1: As a curator, your biggest asset is your individuality. Now that thousands of songs are released daily, you need tools that help you dig deeper, and find sonic connections based on moods and atmospheres instead of genre tags or release dates.
philosophy.p2: Our discovery engine is designed to show you the hidden corners of your unique music taste, letting you appreciate the beauty of tracks that connect even when separated by genres and time; songs that fit together because they were born from similar emotions, just waiting for someone to link them together for the first time.
philosophy.figureAria: Two tracks from different decades, each with its emotion contour; the contours echo the same shape and an orange thread links them — born from similar emotions, linked for the first time by you

statement.bridge: You may already know the atmosphere, groove or energy you want. The difficult part is translating that feeling into the next production decision.
statement.inspiration: Inspiration is a powerful tool that often feels outside of our control. We have an idea for a track, where it should go, the atmosphere it should convey, but have no idea how to bring that vision to life. That's when we get stuck in an endless loop: unable to move forward, if not by ditching an entire project for a fresh start.
statement.pull: But what if you could start from a track that already captures that feeling, and use it as an inspiration to discover completely new creative directions?

block.h2: When you hit a creative block
block.opener: Creative block often appears as repetition: the same eight-bar loop, the same presets, the same sample choices and an arrangement that refuses to move forward.
block.engines: Discovery engines can help you expand your horizons and try something new, but the problem is that most of them are designed to help you find music based on what you already know and what they rely on: genre, artist names, tags, and so on. If you're looking for a specific atmosphere or sonic texture, it can be difficult to describe exactly what you want and results might not be what you need.
block.pull: Sometimes, the best way to find a new idea is to stop searching for exactly what you already have in mind, and start looking for more subtle connections in mood, atmosphere, and emotion.
block.figureAria: A rich sonic atmosphere drawn as layered contours and grain sits above typical discovery fields — genre, artist, tags — which stay empty; the feeling cannot be typed into the form

paths.h2: Use the track that has the feeling to find what comes next
paths.intro: Start with a track that captures the feeling you want to pursue. PYXIS-1 examines the musical relationships behind that reference and surfaces related tracks through groove, energy, harmony, timbre and structure.
paths.engine: PYXIS-1 builds a sonic profile from the reference track across structural, harmonic, rhythmic, timbral and energy characteristics, then surfaces related tracks that can expand your field of reference.
paths.connections: Use those connections as material for study and contrast, then decide how they inform your own arrangement, sound design and production choices.
paths.listIntro: In short, here's how Resomix can help producers at any stage of their career:

stronger.label: Find stronger references
stronger.text: Start with the track that carries the feeling, then explore sonically connected music beyond familiar artists, genres and tags.

patterns.label: Break familiar patterns
patterns.text: Compare how other tracks express related groove, energy, texture or structure through different production choices.

connections.label: Discover unexpected connections
connections.text: Surface relevant tracks outside your usual scene, listening habits or reference library.

reinterpret.text: Transform what you discover through your own arrangement, sound design and production language.

craft.h2: PYXIS-1 surfaces the relationships. You shape the result.
craft.body: Resomix does not generate a track or prescribe a formula. PYXIS-1 surfaces relationships across rhythm, harmony, timbre, structure and energy. You decide what to study, reinterpret, contrast or leave behind in your own production.

final.h2: Bring a reference. Find a new direction.
final.body: Search for or upload a track that captures the groove, atmosphere or energy you are chasing. PYXIS-1 builds its sonic profile and surfaces related music for you to explore.
